text.p: London's venerable Old Vic Theater is back on its feet and losing far less money than rumored, Canadian theatre tycoon David Mirvish said on Monday.
Mirvish and his flamboyant father, "Honest Ed" Mirvish, are selling the Old Vic after rescuing the 179-year-old theatre in 1982 and spending millions of dollars to restore it.
"The Vic is an extraordinary opportunity for somebody who has the time to devote to it," Mirvish said in a telephone interview on Monday.
The Mirvishes are focusing on their Canadian businesses and can no longer devote enough time to the Old Vic, he said.
Aside from the "Honest Ed's" discount store which made the family fortune, father and son operate two Toronto theaters, several restaurants and other businesses.
They have put an $11.25 million (7.5 million British pounds) price on the theatre and nearby Annex. Mirvish said he would not sell it for redevelopment.
"We think it's a pretty reasonable price," he said, declining to comment when asked if he had received offers yet.
Ed Mirvish paid $825,000 (550,000 pounds) for the theater 15 years ago and spent another $3.75 million (2.5 million pounds) to refurbish it.
"He was able to restore it and keep it active and he has put it on its feet again," Mirvish said.

News of the sale led to speculation in some British newspapers that years of heavy losses had prompted the Mirvishes to leave. Some estimates of how much they lost over the last 15 years totalled $40.5 million (27 million pounds).
"People get very excited by big figures. But I can tell you it hasn't reached the top of those estimates," Mirvish said.
The Old Vic was built in 1818 and hosted Britain's best actors for generations before falling on hard times.
Ed Mirvish became interested in the troubled theater after hearing the memories of famous actors who were passing through Toronto years ago.

"Sir John Gielgud and Peter O'Toole would come and they would have lunch with my father. They would all talk about their days at the Old Vic. So what my father bought wasn't only a theatre, but a set of people's dreams," Mirvish said.
Mirvish also rejected reports of a rift between himself and veteran director Sir Peter Hall, whose company will end its residency at the theatre in December.
"Peter has done something extraordinary in the building," he said.
